articles.title: Dani Olmo explains why he left Barcelona for Dinamo Zagreb: ‘Everyone has their own story’
articles.summary: Dani Olmo will face Croatia in a Spain shirt, bringing an interesting personal connection to the international fixture after spending six years developing hi...
articles.body:
Dani Olmo will face Croatia in a Spain shirt, bringing an interesting personal connection to the international fixture after spending six years developing his career at Dinamo Zagreb.

The Barcelona midfielder established himself in Croatian football before returning to Spain, making the encounter a notable one given the role the country played in his rise.

Olmo joined Dinamo Zagreb as a teenager after leaving Barcelona's famed La Masia academy.

His decision to move abroad proved pivotal, giving him regular first-team opportunities and helping him develop into an established international.

His performances in Croatia eventually attracted interest from across Europe, with his progress laying the foundations for his subsequent move to RB Leipzig and eventual return to Barcelona.

Olmo's six years at Zagreb shaped his career

Dinamo Zagreb provided Olmo with the platform to make the transition from promising academy prospect to senior professional.

The midfielder has spoken about the importance of that period in his career, describing the club and the country as places that helped shape him both professionally and personally.

Dani Olmo's return to Croatia will be very emotional. (Photo by Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

"It's going to be a very special game for me.

"I spent six years of my life here, and it's a country that has given me almost everything as a footballer and as a person. These are wonderful feelings."

Olmo also explained why he chose Dinamo when discussing the move that changed the direction of his career.

"Everyone has their own story and their own reasons. What led me to make the decision to come to Dinamo was their interest in having me, the vision they had for me.

"It was one of the best moments I've experienced in my career."

Despite spending a significant part of his development in Croatia, Olmo ultimately pursued his ambition of playing for Spain at international level.

His time in Zagreb made him familiar with Croatian football, but representing Spain remained his priority.

Dani Olmo could have played for Croatia. (Photo by Jose Manuel Alvarez Rey/Getty Images)

The midfielder acknowledged that playing for Croatia was a possibility, but made his international preference clear.

"It was a possibility, but my dream was always to play with Spain".

Olmo's familiarity with Croatian football gives him a personal connection to the opposition, although his importance to Spain will ultimately depend on his role and performance on the pitch.

Beyond his emotional return to the country, the Barcelona midfielder also praised Lamine Yamal's development, highlighting the teenager's growing influence for club and country.

"After each match, he looks better and more mature. At the start of this season, he's helping us both with our play and scoring goals.

"He's a very important player for both Barça and the Spanish national team," he concluded.

articles.title: Real Madrid superstar warned he is ‘losing the affection’ of supporters
articles.summary: Ever since arriving in Spain to sign for Real Madrid, Kylian Mbappe has enjoyed a love-hate relationship with the Spanish media.The Frenchman’s arrival was e...
articles.body:
Ever since arriving in Spain to sign for Real Madrid, Kylian Mbappe has enjoyed a love-hate relationship with the Spanish media.

The Frenchman's arrival was expected to be the signing that propelled a Champions League-winning side to an unstoppable level.

Instead, since Mbappe arrived, Madrid are yet to win a single piece of silverware. He is now facing another wave of criticism in Spain.

Speaking on El Chiringuito , Pedrerol questioned Mbappe's current situation at the Bernabeu and suggested that the connection between the player and Madridistas is beginning to weaken.

"Mbappe is losing the affection of Madridismo," Pedrerol said.

He then questioned how the situation had reached this point given the significance Mbappe attached to finally becoming a Madrid player.

"Hadn't he fulfilled a dream by joining Real Madrid?" he asked.

Mbappe's long-awaited arrival was supposed to represent the completion of a personal ambition as much as a major sporting move for Madrid.

He had secured the move to the Spanish capital after a couple of summers when the move looked possible but did not get over the line.

Madrid supporters demand more than goals

There is an important distinction here. Pedrerol's comments represent his assessment of the mood surrounding Mbappe.

It is not an actual suggestion that Madrid supporters as a whole have turned against the forward.

At Real Madrid, producing extraordinary numbers does not automatically guarantee an emotional connection with the Bernabeu.

Is Kylian Mbappe fully loved by the Santiago Bernabeu? (Photo by Burak Kara/Getty Images)

Supporters also respond to sacrifice, availability and the sense of putting the club above everything and everyone else, and this is true even for a player of Mbappe's status.

Pedrerol also had a strong message for manager Jose Mourinho, who is another important part of this situation.

Managing Mbappe cannot simply be about extracting goals. Mourinho must ensure that one of his most important players feels completely connected to the project.

Mbappe has more than enough quality to silence this chatter in a couple of games. However, he needs to rethink his relationship with the Bernabeu.

Ultimately, it all hinges on how much success and silverware Mbappe is able to bring to the Spanish capital, and it remains to be seen how things play out.

articles.title: 86 to 101: Virat Kohli's final ODI window to break Sachin Tendulkar's century record
articles.summary: Virat Kohli is 15 centuries away from becoming the first batter to reach 101 international hundreds, with ODI cricket now his only route to Sachin Tendulkar'...
articles.body:
It was the semi-final of the 2023 World Cup when Virat Kohli scored his 50th ODI century in front of Sachin Tendulkar, surpassing his idol's record of 49 hundreds in the format. That innings put another Tendulkar record within Kohli's reach. Tendulkar's 100 international centuries remain the benchmark, leaving Kohli with a chance to become the first batter to reach 101. But the equation changed when Kohli retired from Test cricket on May 12, 2025. With his T20I career already over, ODI cricket became his only remaining route to Tendulkar's record. Now, with the 2027 World Cup less than a year away, Kohli has 86 international centuries - 14 short of equalling Tendulkar and 15 away from surpassing him. His latest hundred, a 139 not out against West Indies in the first ODI of the recently concluded series, was followed by 29 in the second match and a golden duck in the third. So how many opportunities does Kohli have left, and can he turn them into the 15 centuries he needs to move past Tendulkar's 100?

India currently have 11 confirmed bilateral ODIs scheduled before the 2027 World Cup - five against New Zealand, three against Sri Lanka and three against Zimbabwe. India's World Cup campaign will begin against Australia in Cape Town on October 7, 2027. The new FTP could add another six-match ODI series in South Africa in the weeks before the World Cup, giving India a chance to acclimatise to conditions ahead of the tournament. However, that series is not part of the confirmed schedule as of yet.

The Asia Cup is another part of the picture. The 2027 tournament is scheduled to be played in Bangladesh from June 18 to July 4 and is expected to return to the ODI format. A detailed fixture list has not been announced, but based on the 2023 format, India could play up to six matches if they reach the final. The World Cup itself will have five group-stage matches and if the team reaches the Super 7, they will play six more matches, with a semi-final and final to follow if they go all the way. A finalist could therefore play a maximum of 13 matches at the tournament. That leaves Kohli with 11 confirmed bilateral ODIs before the World Cup, with the Asia Cup providing additional opportunities before the tournament. For Kohli, the target remains 15 centuries.

India or overseas? The recent pattern in Kohli's centuries

Kohli's recent ODI numbers are markedly different at home and overseas. In his last 32 ODI matches in India, he has scored nine centuries. In his last 32 overseas ODIs, he has scored three - in Dubai, Chattogram and Colombo.

That split comes into focus with India scheduled to play five ODIs in New Zealand before the World Cup. Kohli's overall record overseas, though, is substantial. He has scored 27 of his 55 ODI centuries outside India. Bangladesh is his most productive overseas country, with six centuries, followed by Sri Lanka and Australia with five each. He has four in the West Indies, three in South Africa and one each in New Zealand, England, Zimbabwe and the UAE.

Sri Lanka remains one of Kohli's most productive opponents. Kohli has scored 10 ODI centuries against Sri Lanka, his highest tally against any opponent. The three-match series in December will be played in India, with the ODIs scheduled for December 13, 16 and 19. Zimbabwe follow with three matches on January 3, 6 and 9.

2027 World Cup: Kohli's final shot at Sachin's record

Kohli's World Cup record gives him a strong base to build on. In 37 World Cup matches, he has scored 1,795 runs at an average of 59.83, with five centuries and 12 half-centuries.

The 2023 edition was his most productive World Cup. He scored 765 runs, including three centuries and six half-centuries, and finished as the tournament's leading run-scorer. It was also the tournament in which he scored his 50th ODI century, moving past Tendulkar's record of 49.

Kohli has already crossed 15000 ODI runs, becoming only the second batter after Tendulkar to reach the mark. He did so in his 303rd innings. With Test and T20I cricket behind him, every international century Kohli scores from here will come in ODIs. He has also said that the 2027 World Cup will be his last World Cup for India. Fifteen hundreds remain between Kohli and 101.

articles.title: Explaining Lionel Messi's special final Argentina jersey and if fans can buy iconic shirt
articles.summary: In a match fit for footballing royalty, Messi will be draped in distinctive — and elegant — robes.
articles.body:
Lionel Messi 's retirement from international play has been a long time coming.

The Argentine supernova first announced his intention to step away after in June 2016, moments after La Albiceleste fell to Chile in the Copa America final. He reversed course two months later, saying he had business to finish with his beloved country.

Argentines around the world have been rejoicing in the decade since. Messi picked up two Copa Americas and the 2022 World Cup, capturing the competition's Golden Ball in the process.

Now, it's time for the real thing. The 39-year-old will take part in his final Argentina fixture on Tuesday, facing off with Benin at Estadio Monumental.

In a match fit for footballing royalty, Messi will be draped in new — and rather elegant — robes. Here's what you need to know about the special jersey Messi and his teammates will wear when they take to the field on Tuesday night.

Explaining Lionel Messi's special final Argentina jersey

Argentina's kit for Messi final match features numerous wrinkles. The bespoke offering, crafted by Adidas, features wide striping as compared to the slimmer pattern that has adorned most of the country's jerseys during the Messi years. Cloaked within the blue-and-white design is sun-like regalia that dances on the front and back of the kit, inspired by the "Sol de Mayo" emblem that resides on the middle of the South American nation's flag.

Messi's "M" logo replaces the Adidas logo in the attire. It is caked in a luminous gold, as is the diminutive playmaker's iconic No. 10. Given Messi's performances in La Albiceleste colors over the years, the hue seems appropriate.

A longtime Adidas athlete, Messi will complete the look with custom white-and-blue cleats. If Tuesday is, indeed, Messi's coronation, than he is certainly dressed to impress.

The kit made its public debut — if you can call it that — when Adidas unveiled a 30-meter-long installation of the look in Rosario, Messi's hometown.

Where to buy Messi's final Argentina jersey

Those hoping to get hands on Messi's final Argentina kit can find it in a variety of outlets, including Fanatics , Dick's Sporting Goods and JD Sports . The jersey is also available on Adidas' official website , although its availability appears to be waning.

articles.title: How Messi's struggle to emerge from Maradona's shadow sealed his eternal glory in Argentina
articles.summary: Lionel Messi has come a long way in his Argentina career — but he'll go down as one of the nation's greats.
articles.body:
No one does a mass outpouring quite like Argentina soccer fans.

Take the estimated five million who poured onto the streets of Buenos Aires to celebrate the national team finally winning a third World Cup in 2022, Lionel Messi 's long-awaited finest hour.

Or the millions who took to town squares across the country when the nation's eternal icon Diego Maradona died in November 2020. Ongoing coronavirus restrictions never stood a chance.

On Tuesday, at River Plate's Estadio Monumental in the nation's capital, similar emotions will mesh. The stakes aren't as high, but there will be waves of joy and sadness when Messi plays in Argentina colours for the final time against Benin on Tuesday.

The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner is bowing out on top at the right time. It will feel like a sporting death as tears are shed, but what a sporting life. Messi has the eternal gratitude and love of a soccer nation quite unlike any other.

After inspiring Argentina to glory in 2022 and sparkling at the 2026 World Cup – eight goals, four assists and evergreen brilliance – Messi is assured of a lifetime of affection unimaginable to most mortals.

What makes this all the more remarkable is that it was never guaranteed. Indeed, for a decent chunk of Messi's international career – at a time when he was the consensus best player on the planet – the universal love of his homeland didn't even seem likely.

"Football, for us, isn't rational . Even though we didn't invent it, even though we're not the best at it, even though we don't always win, even though our organizations are a ship adrift," Mauricio Codocea wrote on these pages after the 2022 World Cup final. "The thing about us Argentinians and football is that we feel it more than anyone else. We feel it like Maradona did. We feel it like Messi does."

This is the story of Messi's long walk home to the country he left as a child, how he took that country on his shoulders as an adult and felt it as much as every single one of them.

Turning out in his home province at a major tournament for Argentina, Messi was introduced as "the best in the world" by the stadium announcer at Santa Fe's Estadio Brigadier General Estanislao Lopez.

The response was polite applause. Fair enough: perhaps the locals were nervous following a lacklustre opening draw against Bolivia in the 2011 Copa America. There was little room for further error with Colombia in town.

Next up, after Messi's No. 10, was the Albiceleste's No. 11. "The player of the people, Carlos Tevez!" The masses roared. This outpouring of affection for Tevez on Messi's turf offered a snapshot of the discussions and presumptions over Argentina's star player as he entered his prime years.

His otherworldly quality was beyond question. Messi had just won his second Champions League in three seasons at Barcelona and was two Ballons d'Or into an unbroken four-year run. But he increasingly came up short in the popular imagination in terms of intangible and shifting measures of authenticity.

A century ago, Argentina was the birthplace of what might be referred to today — derisively or otherwise — as football hipsters. Writers working for the influential sports magazine El Grafico wrote in romantic terms about how the sport brought to South America as a well-mannered British game had developed a uniquely Argentinian edge as it evolved within burgeoning working-class communities. This amounted to greater cunning, improvisation and trickery, underpinned by a sleight-of-hand if required.

The writer Ricardo Lorenzo, better known by his pseudonym of Borocoto, felt this democratisation of football made it as fundamental to the Argentine experience and identity as tango music. As recounted by Jonathan Wilson in his book on the history of football in Argentina, Angels With Dirty Faces , in 1928 Borocoto described raising a statue to the imagined inventor of dribbling.

"A pibe (a kid/urchin) with a dirty face, a mane of hair rebelling against the comb; with intelligent, roving, trickster and persuasive eyes and a sparkling gaze that seems to hint at a picaresque laugh that does not quite manage to form on his mouth, full of small teeth that might be worn down through eating yesterday's bread," Borocoto began.

"His trousers are a few roughly sewn patches; his vest with Argentinian stripes, with a very low neck and with many holes eaten out by the invisible mice of use. His stance must be characteristic; it must seem as if he is dribbling with a rag ball. This is important: the ball cannot be any other. A rag ball and preferably bound by an old sock."

For all his inimitable gifts, as a middle-class kid from Rosario, Messi had not had to spend too much time chewing on yesterday's bread and kicking around a rag ball in careworn clothing, even before Barcelona and their European riches uprooted Leo and his family, bringing them to Catalonia when he was 13 years old. Tevez, on the other hand, fitted this archetype like a glove, with his rampant playing style, unruly appearance and tough upbringing on the dangerous streets of Fuerte Apache all part of the same whole.

As Wilson points out, Borocoto did an eerily excellent job of describing Diego Maradona more than half a decade before his 1980s heyday. El pibe de oro — the golden boy — was one of Maradona's most enduring nicknames in Argentina. His upbringing was pure Tevez and he scrapped his way to riches on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean, as opposed to being hand-picked for stardom.

These comparisons became tougher after Maradona's unexpected move into Messi's orbit. Despite minimal and largely unimpressive coaching experience, Diego was appointed Argentina boss in 2008. It wasn't that the two men clashed; on the contrary, they had a close and warm personal relationship.

Maradona made Messi the focal point of his team, playing where he would have played in a 4-3-1-2 as the difference-making No. 10. But Argentina were hammered by Germany in the quarterfinals and the man who overtook the World Cup's all-time leading scorer Miroslav Klose last summer played five matches without scoring a goal.

The 2011 Copa also ended in disappointment, with Argentina drawing three of their four games before going out on penalties to Uruguay in the quarterfinals. Shootouts would become an ever-prevalent part of the story, but the gap between the calibre of Argentina's European-based superstars and the national team's level of achievement was far too jarring for fans during the period. When it came to Barcelona icon Messi, there was a chasm between what he was and what Maradona had been.

"While some people always supported him, a large portion of the public was very critical of him in his early days, and even a little later with the Albiceleste," says Renzo Desaunet of Sporting News Argentina. "This was due to many factors, but mainly to the high expectations Argentines place on their stars—especially since he was so often compared to Maradona. Diego's flamboyant personality was directly proportional to Leo's shyness—a humble young man who grew up in Spain, something many have held against him, as if that made him any less Argentine!

"Failing to achieve goals with the national team—while excelling at Barcelona—led to mounting criticism, to the point where he was singled out for the slightest thing, such as occasionally not singing the national anthem. He may not have performed at his best for Argentina in the occasional tournament, but there was no doubt that he gave it his all."

It was the soundtrack of the World Cup in Brazil and the Brazilians hated it. Perhaps not quite as much as getting seismically demolished by Germany 7-1 in the semi-finals, but it was a close-run thing.

Vocal Argentina fans decamped to their neighbouring country en masse. Surely, they felt, it was their time. Some estimates suggest in excess of 200,000 made the pilgrimage over the course of the tournament, many travelling without tickets and winging it: staying in schools, sleeping on the streets or finding a place to crash in the favelas.

The man bearing the most responsibility for this odyssey was Messi. He was 26 when the competition kicked off, the age Maradona was in 1986. He was Argentina's captain and No.10, and accompanied by five teammates from that Youth World Cup triumph of 2005. Together, they were ready to fulfil the promises made back then.

The travelling Albiceleste caravan delighted in leaning into this symbolism. Their tournament anthem of Brasil decime que se siente (Brazil, tell me how it feels), hollered to the tune of 'Bad Moon Rising' by Creedence Clearwater Revival, ended thusly:

"With Messi, you're going to see — the cup, he's going to bring it home. Maradona is greater than Pele."

After a disappointing season at Barcelona without a major honour, Messi started like a house on fire. He scored five in three games in the group stage, with two genuine goal-of-the-tournament contenders against Bosnia & Herzegovina and Nigeria. He'd laid the platform to do what Diego did in 1986.

But he couldn't build on it. Fatigue seemed to grip Messi in the knockout stages and he became increasingly peripheral. There was a superb assist for Angel Di Maria to avert penalties against Switzerland before Gonzalo Higuain's early goal saw Belgium dispatched by the same 1-0 scoreline. A suffocating 0-0 draw against the Netherlands in the semifinals ended in a penalty shootout victory for Alejandro Sabella's side.

Those gruelling, tight matches preceded another in the final, where Mario Gotze's extra-time goal ended Messi's dream after 90 goalless minutes.

"For me, the national team is over," Messi said. "I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion. It's been four finals [including the 2007 Copa America], I tried. It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over.

"I think this is best for everyone. First of all for me, then for everyone. I think there are a lot of people who want this, who obviously are not satisfied, as we are not satisfied reaching a final and not winning it. It's very hard, but the decision is taken. Now I will not try more and there will be no going back."

Those were Messi's comments after his shootout failure in the Copa America Centenario final at MetLife Stadium, which contributed to Chile walking away with the trophy. He shed tears on the field. Argentina also lost in the Copa final via the same means to Chile in 2015, that unusual quirk of the calendar meaning La Albiceleste had lost three finals in agonizing circumstances in the space of three years, leaving Messi still without a major trophy.

"In Argentine culture, finishing in second place often looks worse than not competing at all or being mediocre," says Agustin Aboy from Sporting News Argentina. "Three consecutive losses in finals made the glory look impossible, even for Messi."

There were other factors behind an ultimately short-lived international retirement. The playing squad as a whole had been broadly dissatisfied with the Argentine Football Association's (AFA) provisions on international duty for some time. Nevertheless, the sight of Leo being so distraught that he could not bear it anymore disabused anyone of the notion that the kid who moved to Barcelona as a young teen didn't care about Argentina. If anything, he cared too much.

There was an outpouring back home, pleading with Messi to overturn his decision. He did so soon enough, rejoining Argentina's struggling campaign to qualify for the 2018 World Cup. They we staring at elimination when they fell 1-0 behind to Ecuador at Quito's punishing altitude. Messi responded with an otherworldly hat-trick, fixing the problem himself in a way that only he could.

Argentina were bound for Russia, the Messi generation granted a final chance to make good on their promise. There was even a top-tier coach in position, with Jorge Sampaoli abandoning a burgeoning career in Europe to take the reins. But Argentina were a rabble.

They drew with Iceland, a game notable for one of Messi's most infamous penalty-kick failures, and were hammered by Croatia. Messi scored a majestic goal in a breathless 2-1 win over Nigeria, despite the squad effectively being in open mutiny against Sampaoli at this point.

A chaotic Argentina side ran out of road in a rollercoaster 4-3 defeat to France in the last-16, a scoreline tempered by Sergio Aguero's goal deep into stoppage time. It was the end of the road for a team that flattered to deceive. But, crucially, Messi wasn't done. Not this time.

From the ashes of their Russian expedition, against all odds, rose one of the most successful international teams in history. Lionel Scaloni was left as the last man standing from Sampaoli's backroom staff. Largely on the grounds of being cheap and available, the AFA gave him the job.

A third-place finish at the 2019 Copa ensured Scaloni could be more than a stopgap. Two years later, at a behind-closed-doors Maracanã, Argentina beat their great rivals Brazil to win the Copa America. Angel Di Maria, one of Messi's last remaining allies from the golden generation, got the goal and the monkey was off their back. They had momentum, took it to Qatar and you know the rest.

Any player who produced the tournaments Messi did in 2022 and 2026 – not to mention retaining the Copa in 2024 in between — would be remembered as an all-time great of international soccer. It is not only his inimitable greatness that separates him from the rest, but also the struggle he had to endure to prevail.

"Through that long and turbulent road, the story had an even sweeter ending," Agustin says. "Today, Messi now enjoys that something almost no one in Argentina ever achieves, not even the biggest legends in any discipline: he is beyond debate."

articles.title: Leny Yoro: French media deliver verdict on Man United star after 4-1 Belgium win
articles.summary: Manchester United defender Leny Yoro marked his senior international debut in France’s 4-1 win over Belgium. The French defender started the game and was sol...
articles.body:
Manchester United defender Leny Yoro marked his senior international debut in France's 4-1 win over Belgium. The French defender started the game and was solid overall, helping his team come back from a goal down to secure a valuable victory.

Yoro was called up to international duty by new manager Zinedine Zidane following an injury to Ibrahima Konaté. The United starlet has endured a mixed start to the new campaign, during which he has struggled for game time.

Yoro has started two games and has also covered at right-back on a couple of occasions. Unfortunately, he has looked shaky, but that did not stop Zidane from taking a chance on him in a crucial game.

Paired alongside Maxence Lacroix, the 20-year-old managed to hold his own against Belgium and even earned praise from his manager. French media have now provided their verdict on the defender.

Foot Mercato gave Yoro a rating of 6 out of 10, stating: "Like Restes, the Manchester United player made his debut for Les Bleus as a starter. The former Lille player took advantage of the absence of Upamecano (suspended) and Jacquet (hamstring injury) to play tonight, having been called up to the French squad following Konaté's withdrawal."

"And to say the least, he certainly made the most of his opportunity. Strong in one-on-one challenges, the new international was incisive in his interventions and precise in his build-up play. Although he was not involved in Belgium's opening goal, he put in a more than solid performance."

The French defender also earned a 6/10 rating from RMC Sport , who noted: "The defender made a point of pushing forward as often as possible, focusing particularly on the right flank. He also remained alert against Lukaku. It was through these runs that he really managed to set himself apart from Jacquet."

Yoro also earned praise from Get Football News France , who handed him another 6/10, adding: "The Manchester United centre-back hardly put a foot wrong and played his part in cutting the transmissions to Romelu Lukaku. Not as impressive as Jérémy Jacquet, but a very decent start to international life nevertheless."

Yoro was heavily involved under former head coach Ruben Amorim, but found game time hard to come by following Michael Carrick's arrival in January. Last season, the English manager only opted for Yoro when either Harry Maguire or Lisandro Martinez were injured or suspended.

This season, the Frenchman only has two appearances in the Premier League, both of which have been from the bench. His only starts have been in the 4-0 win over Sabah in the Champions League and the disastrous 3-2 defeat at the hands of Brighton & Hove Albion in the EFL Cup third round.

United are expected to push for defensive reinforcements in 2027, and recent reports suggest have their eyes on Tottenham Hotspur's Micky van de Ven. The Dutchman's possible arrival could spell trouble for Yoro at Old Trafford.

Meanwhile, it has also been suggested that Amorim is ready for a reunion with the Frenchman at AC Milan.

With Maguire on the wrong side of 30 and Martinez's contract expiring next summer, it is high time for Carrick to put more trust in Yoro. The Frenchman has all the attributes to be a hit at Old Trafford and all he needs is extended playing time.

articles.title: Últimas noches con Modric
articles.standfirst: El capitán de Croacia, en su paso gradual a la condición de ex, recoge lo que sembró en una carrera modélica. Ganó mucho, nunca dejó de competir, y no se le conoce un solo enemigo.
articles.summary: El capitán de Croacia, en su paso gradual a la condición de ex, recoge lo que sembró en una carrera modélica. Ganó mucho, nunca dejó de competir, y no se le conoce un solo enemigo.
articles.body: En estos días de selecciones comprobamos que se acaba una era. La fuga de Cristiano Ronaldo en la concentración de Portugal podría ser el epílogo triste a la mayor leyenda del fútbol luso junto a Eusebio. En manos del crack de Madeira está adecentar, aunque sea parcialmente, el adiós a la selección de su país, la que tanta gloria ha aportado a ambos. No parece fácil, pese a la puerta abierta por el seleccionador, un poco a destiempo. Si Cristiano dio el portazo, debería ser él quien llamase para volver a entrar. Veremos. Y mientras, por oposición, aparece Modric de nuevo en la cartelera. Aún fresca la ovación del Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán la pasada semana, el croata, superadas las cuatro décadas de carné de identidad, conserva el liderazgo y el orgullo de un futbolista en plenitud. Ayer compareció en rueda de Prensa como líder de una selección en un punto crítico. Ya lo hizo tras el 0-7 ante Inglaterra, al frente: “Siento vergüenza por primera vez en 20 años con la selección croata”. En ese tiempo, con la selección y con sus clubes, Modric fue labrando poco a poco una carrera modélica, tan repleta de victorias y títulos como vacía de enemigos.Ese homenaje espontáneo de los aficionados sevillistas, después de tantas batallas contra el RealMadrid, muestran la magnitud de la figura. No fue, además, algo esporádico. Ya le ocurrió cuando aún pertenecía al club blanco.En SanMamés, por ejemplo. Se extiende en los últimos meses la teoría de que los más grandes deben ser ambiciososo, competitivos, ególatras, altaneros. Modric es la demostración aún en activo de que los genios pueden dejar también un legado fuera del campo. PD: CASO NEGREIRA. Semana 190. Dimisiones, 0; ceses, 0. Hace escasos días, el Real Madrid completó su vasto informe a la UEFA, que hizo acuse de recibo, y urgió al organismo europeo a tomar medidas contra el Barcelona por el Caso Negreira. Dicen que nunca es tarde. Pero si el club blanco se hubiese empleado desde el principio de forma tan contundente e inequívoca, no llevaríamos 190 semanas subrayando la gravedad que tiene el mero hecho de pagar durante años a un alto dirigente arbtiral.

articles.title: Lionel Messi is leaving international football with grace. Cristiano Ronaldo could never
articles.summary: Comment: Messi is retiring from international football at the right time as he prepares for his Argentina swan song on Tuesday night
articles.body:
In boxing, some say the classiest way to go out is on your back, staring at the lights. Everyone loves a fairytale ending, but there is a certain closure that comes with bowing out in defeat.

Regardless of what happens in Buenos Aires on Tuesday night, in a friendly against Benin, Lionel Messi will end his Argentina career in a similar vein. The final, overriding taste will be one of loss.

The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner, 39, announced his retirement from international football following the 2026 World Cup. His designated farewell match will be held at the the iconic Estadio Monumental, home of River Plate .

Widely regarded as the greatest footballer of all time, Messi goes out having seen his stock rise even further in the summer . He completely outperformed expectation, even for him, at the World Cup to show that he could still run the show while pushing 40. Eight goals, four assists and, briefly, the tournament's all-time top scorer - before golden boot winner Kylian Mbappe snatched that accolade - represented a truly remarkable output for the Argentinian magician, even if it all came to nothing.

After guiding the defending champions to a second successive World Cup final, he was unable to repeat his heroics of Qatar to end on the highest of highs. In fact, it was the lowest of lows. Argentina's post-match brawl sparked by Leandro Paredes and co. cast a cloud of shame over him and an entire nation, though Messi was not an innocent party in Argentina's performance of disgrace.

In the aftermath of Enzo Fernandez ragdolling Pau Cubarsi to get himself sent off in second-half stoppage time, he tried to level the playing field after Marc Cucurella spoke while covering his mouth, appealing to the referee to produce a red under the "Vinicius law" - something that had been written into the game courtesy of compatriot Gianluca Prestianni's alleged racism . It was a desperate abandonment of sporting integrity from a footballing marvel made out to be immune to mistakes.

His efforts both in this regard and with the football at his feet proved fruitless. Spain ran out deserving winners against Argentina's anti-football in extra time.

Messi's tears on New Jersey shores spoke to an inevitability. Though with less individual ignominy than Diego Maradona before him, whose international retirement followed a failed drug test at the 1994 World Cup, Messi was similarly hurtling towards the end of his tenure as Argentina's heroic figurehead . That was rubber stamped by the passing of his father and agent, Jorge , at the age of 68 after a long illness.

Six weeks after the final, Messi confirmed his retirement. "There isn't much time left, chapters come to a close, and this is one that hurts me deeply," he wrote on Instagram. "I love, have loved, and will always love being part of the national team. I've given it my all, I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are some really great young players coming through behind me who deserve their chance."

It felt right. After 21 years, 207 appearances, 125 goals and 68 assists, there will be just one more game. An international career categorised by pain and perseverance, he bows out with a World Cup, two Copa Americas and an Olympic gold medal to his name; though in contrast to his club success, he more often fell at the final hurdle. Runners-up medals at two World Cups and three Copa Americas, heartbreak regularly prevailed during the Messi era - something that eventually became the rocket fuel for the current crop of players, dedicated to deliver him those titles before it was too late. Lionel Scaloni built a team that would first and foremost die for Messi; that team won Argentina's first World Cup since Mexico '86 and third overall.

He retires having achieved what he wanted, and he retires an undisputed hero. The same cannot be said for his "GOAT debate" counterpart, if you can even call him that anymore, with Cristiano Ronaldo 's international career at risk of coming to the most pathetic of ends thanks to his latest strop.

After at least two years of being a hinderance to the team's efforts , taking up a starting spot that should be going to someone younger and more deserving, Ronaldo opted against using the natural end of the World Cup cycle to hang up his international boots and instead remained in the fold. That was until he quit the squad after being an unused substitute for the first time in 18 years for a Nations League clash with Norway; one Portugal won, with his replacement Goncalo Ramos scoring the winner. "In due time, I will tell the truth to all Portuguese people about the reasons that motivated my departure from the national team," he wrote on social media. Cue a fourth Piers Morgan interview.

The thing is, nobody actually cares anymore. Ronaldo is like that self-important wet flannel you kind of know that posts: "Deleting my social media, had enough of fake people. If you need me, text me." Except he's not 14, he's 41. It's for that reason we don't want to give him anymore attention because, like a problematic child, it only encourages this behaviour.

Instead, we look to his rival, who has watched silently as Ronaldo hammered another nail into the coffin that is his "GOAT" argument. Ronaldo's legacy is growing damaged by the month. Messi's continues to glisten, despite being fresh off failure on the grandest of stages, both on an individual and team level. He has more than enough credit in the bank for that to be forgiven.

In Buenos Aires, more tears will be shed; overflowing gratitude, pride and immense sadness. But there will be no anger, no disappointment, no ill-feeling. Messi has defined an era of football to a point of deification in his homeland. He leaves at the right time, with dignity and his head held high.

articles.title: Stephen Welsh: Born into Celtic, made at Motherwell, defender comes of age with Scotland
articles.summary: It takes talent, resilience and good fortune in finding managers who believe in you, but dreams can come true. Stephen Welsh is living proof of it, writes Tom English.
articles.body:
On the day he left Celtic after "18 years of ups and downs", Stephen Welsh posted a classy video on social media thanking the club for everything they'd done for him.

The footage featured a clip of him as a child in a Celtic jersey, playing indoor football with his mates with the number 18 and the name 'Lennon' on the back.

He smiles at the camera, held by his mum, and says he scored a goal. Welsh looks like the most contented kid on the planet. He's all grown up now at 26, hard-bitten by the reality of professional sport, but meet him at Lesser Hampden on Monday afternoon and that same smile is there. Maybe not the same boyish innocence but certainly the same love for what he's doing in the game.

From bit-part player at Celtic to a turning point season at Motherwell under his greatest influence Jens Berthel Askou to top of the Championship with Swansea, to three caps for his country. Impressive ones, too. Composed in his defending, accurate in his distribution, convincing in his partnership with fellow newcomer Luis Binks. Much has changed in his life.

Playing for Scotland is one thing but winning is quite another. How did it feel on Saturday night in Skopje when the last whistle sounded and his first win was put on the board?

"A bit of relief," he says. "We felt there could have been a lot more goals. Five or six and you probably couldn't have argued. To get your first win under your belt is a good feeling. Hopefully it pushes us on now."

The final act of this international window comes on Tuesday when Slovenia arrive at Hampden (19:45 BST), a chance to make up for last week's nightmarish experience against the Swiss, a game reduced to a non-event after Jack Hendry's early red card. Scotland battled away, but lost 3-0.

A "sore one", he says. "We had to suffer for a good 80-90 minutes," he explains. "That can take its toll mentally but we showed how strong we are going into North Macedonia.

"It will mean a lot for the squad, for the manager to come back home and put on a good performance and finish the camp with a win. You need to keep building on that. That's the standard that we want to set."

Welsh's story starts at Celtic, a product of their academy who turned down overtures from Udinese and Toulouse in his time. He wanted to stay and fight for his place but it was all stop-start.

After making his debut in the spring of 2020, Celtic kept signing centre-halves - Carl Starfelt and Liam Scales, Cameron Carter-Vickers and Yuki Kobayashi, Moritz Jenz and Maik Nawrocki, Gustaf Lagerbielke and Auston Trusty.

He played 70 games in total. It wasn't enough. "It's not easy but at a club like Celtic, they always want to improve, bring in more players because that keeps the competition," Welsh says. "It's football. You're not guaranteed to play even though you want to.

"For your boyhood club, to play every game, would have been the best-case scenario. Unfortunately, that didn't happen. I'm a big boy, I can accept that players are going to play in front of you. That's fair enough."

Humble Gilmour happy with new role as 50th cap beckons

Pocognoli backs Scotland strikers for 'must-win' game against Slovenia

Challenging years, though. A time for mental fortitude.

"That's probably the thing that people don't see," he remarks. "What you need then is a good support group around you, good family, good friends. My agent was excellent for me. They just need to be there. That's the main thing, just be there.

"Psychologically, it can affect players but I don't think it affected me too much. I never took anything personally. That's just the way it goes. The best players, technically, probably don't [always] get to the top. It's the players that are mentally strong.

"Look at John [McGinn] and Robbo [Andy Robertson]. The mentality that they have. They're obviously fantastic footballers but it's the mental strength as well. To churn out performances every week, to turn up in good shape, to be ready to play tactically, technically, physically and mentally. That's the biggest challenge."

Podcast: McGinn, McTominay, Robertson: Are Scotland's greats undroppable?

In an effort to get game time, Welsh signed a loan with Mechelen in Belgium before making the move of his life to Motherwell. He says he had one conversation with Berthel Askou and he was hooked.

"Going from Celtic to Motherwell doesn't look the most brilliant move in the world, but…" it made him. "How he coached me on and off the pitch, it was top level," Welsh recalls. "I didn't realise how good a decision it was to join Motherwell until close to the end of the season, when you start getting the recognition. I would say that's all down to how he coached me."

Players speak about Berthel Askou with something approaching awe and Welsh is no different. "He just gave me pure belief," he says. "He made the game so simple for the team and that helped me as well.

"Every single day, so detailed, how he analysed teams, how he analysed specific ways of playing against teams. The biggest influence on my career by a distance. He completely changed how my career path turned out."

The move to Swansea - his Motherwell pal EIijah Just is alongside him - was another good decision. A manager, Vitor Matos, who appreciates him. A dressing room that's talented and driven. Top of the league after eight games. So far, so good.

Like Berthel Askou and Matos, new Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli trusts him, too. Welsh always had it in the back of his mind that if he kept going with Motherwell and then Swansea that something might happen with his country.

It has - and he's seized the moment. Three caps should become four on Tuesday. If one win becomes two then we might be reminded of his smiling younger self again.

It takes talent, resilience and good fortune in finding managers who believe in you, but dreams can come true. Welsh is living proof of it.

Llamado de urgencia tras la lesión de Ferran, se quedó fuera de los 23 en Oviedo ante la República Checa y repite ante Coacia en Split. Después de hace cinco de los 13 goles de España a San Marino, Carlos Espí cambió el equipo de David Gordo por el de Luis de la Fuente. Pero el jugador del Real Madrid no jugará esta tarde ante Rumania en Ibiza ni lo hará con la absoluta en Ibiza. El seleccionador ha dado continuidad al delantero del Espanyol. Roberto debutó ante los checos, lleva toda la ventana con la selección y en los dos primeros patidos se quedó fuera.
